Multistate model and treatment switching

Source: vignettes/switching.Rmd
switching.Rmd
library(DesignComplexSurvival)

ms_model() defines the model of one treatment group. The patient moves between five states with piecewise constant intensities:

  1. progression-free and alive,
  2. progressed without switch,
  3. switched,
  4. dead,
  5. progression-free after a switch before progression (used only when switch_pre is positive).

Progression-free survival (PFS) is the time to leave the progression-free states 1 and 5, and overall survival (OS) is the time to enter state 4. Before progression the intensities are functions of the time since randomization; after progression they are functions of the time since progression or since randomization (the clock, see below). Dropout is independent of the event process. This article shows how switching at, after and before progression enters the model, and how the options change OS, PFS and the power of the log-rank test.

Switching at and after progression

In the control group the hazard of progression is 0.10 per month in the first 4 months and 0.08 afterwards. At progression, 30 percent of the patients switch to the experimental treatment, and the others may switch later with a hazard of 0.04 per month. After progression the hazard of death is 0.06 without switch and 0.035 after a switch. The treatment group has a lower hazard of progression and no switching.

ctl_sw <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.10, 0.08), death = 0.01,
                   switch_prob = 0.3, death_prog = 0.06, switch_rate = 0.04,
                   death_switch = 0.035, dropout = 0.003)
trt_sw <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.06, 0.05), death = 0.008,
                   death_prog = 0.055, dropout = 0.003)
pr <- ms_prob(ctl_sw, time = c(6, 12, 24))
pr
#>   time progression_free progressed  switched      dead
#> 1    6        0.5379444  0.2102858 0.1417831 0.1099867
#> 2   12        0.3134862  0.2176410 0.2161661 0.2527068
#> 3   24        0.1064585  0.1329666 0.2539857 0.5065892

The state probabilities do not include dropout. At 24 months, 25 percent of the control patients are alive after a switch and 51 percent have died.

The control group without switching has the same intensities with switch_prob and switch_rate set to zero. The OS curves of the three models:

ctl_ns <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.10, 0.08), death = 0.01,
                   death_prog = 0.06, dropout = 0.003)
models <- list(control = ctl_sw, control_no_switch = ctl_ns, treatment = trt_sw)
tt <- seq(0, 48, by = 1)
os <- sapply(models, function(m) ms_surv(m, tt, "os")$surv)
matplot(tt, os, type = "l", lty = 1:3, col = 1, ylim = c(0, 1),
        xlab = "Months since randomization", ylab = "Overall survival")
legend("topright", c("Control with switching", "Control without switching",
                     "Treatment"), lty = 1:3, bty = "n")

median_os <- function(m) {
  stats::uniroot(function(t) ms_surv(m, t, "os")$surv - 0.5, c(0.1, 500))$root
}
med <- sapply(models, median_os)
round(med, 1)
#>           control control_no_switch         treatment 
#>              23.6              20.5              26.6

The median OS is 23.6 months in the control group with switching, 20.5 months without switching and 26.6 months in the treatment group. PFS does not depend on the switching after progression.

The design has an interim analysis at 60 percent of the final 300 OS events and 500 patients enrolled at 25 per month:

looks <- ms_looks("os", fraction = c(0.6, 1))
pw <- ms_power(ms_scenario(ctl_sw, trt_sw, accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25)),
               n = 500, looks = looks, test = ms_test(), events = 300)
pw_ns <- ms_power(ms_scenario(ctl_ns, trt_sw, accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 25)),
                  n = 500, looks = looks, test = ms_test(), events = 300)
c(switching = pw$power, no_switching = pw_ns$power)
#>    switching no_switching 
#>    0.2205938    0.8426871

Switching to the experimental treatment in the control group moves the hazard ratio for OS towards 1: the power is 0.221 with switching and 0.843 without.

The clock of the post-progression intensities

The post-progression intensities are piecewise constant on intervals that start at time_post. With clock = "reset" (the default) the intervals refer to the time since progression (a semi-Markov model); with clock = "forward" they refer to the time since randomization (a Markov model). In the following model the hazard of death after progression is 0.08 in the first 6 months and 0.04 afterwards:

m_reset <- ms_model(prog = 0.08, death = 0.01, time_post = c(0, 6),
                    death_prog = c(0.08, 0.04))
m_fwd <- ms_model(prog = 0.08, death = 0.01, time_post = c(0, 6),
                  death_prog = c(0.08, 0.04), clock = "forward")
tc <- c(12, 24, 36)
os_clock <- sapply(list(reset = m_reset, forward = m_fwd),
                   function(m) ms_surv(m, tc, "os")$surv)
rownames(os_clock) <- paste("month", tc)
round(os_clock, 3)
#>          reset forward
#> month 12 0.709   0.756
#> month 24 0.458   0.525
#> month 36 0.290   0.344

With the reset clock, a patient who progresses at month 10 has the hazard 0.08 until month 16. With the forward clock the hazard is 0.04 from month 6 on, so this patient has the hazard 0.04 at once, and OS is longer. PFS is the same under both clocks. When the post-progression intensities are constant, the two clocks give the same model.

The death hazard after a switch

By default (switch_clock = "same") the hazard death_switch is measured on the clock of the other post-progression intensities. With switch_clock = "switch" it is measured from the time of the switch. In the following model the patients switch after progression with a hazard of 0.05 per month, and the death hazard after a switch is 0.03 in the first interval and 0.05 afterwards:

m_same <- ms_model(prog = 0.08, death = 0.01, time_post = c(0, 6),
                   death_prog = c(0.08, 0.06), switch_rate = 0.05,
                   death_switch = c(0.03, 0.05))
m_since <- ms_model(prog = 0.08, death = 0.01, time_post = c(0, 6),
                    death_prog = c(0.08, 0.06), switch_rate = 0.05,
                    death_switch = c(0.03, 0.05), switch_clock = "switch")
os_switch <- sapply(list(same = m_same, since_switch = m_since),
                    function(m) ms_surv(m, tc, "os")$surv)
rownames(os_switch) <- paste("month", tc)
round(os_switch, 3)
#>           same since_switch
#> month 12 0.711        0.714
#> month 24 0.430        0.440
#> month 36 0.246        0.257

A patient who switches 4 months after progression has the hazard 0.03 for 2 months with "same" and for 6 months with "switch". With clock = "reset" the two choices differ only for switches after progression (switch_rate); switches at progression (switch_prob) start both clocks at the same time.

An accelerated failure time effect of the switch

With switch_af, the switch has an accelerated failure time effect: the remaining time after the switch is the remaining time without switch divided by switch_af, as in the rank preserving structural failure time model of Robins and Tsiatis (1991). A value below 1 prolongs survival. When death_prog is constant, this is the same as the death hazard switch_af * death_prog after the switch:

m_af1 <- ms_model(prog = 0.08, death = 0.01, death_prog = 0.06,
                  switch_rate = 0.05, switch_af = 0.7)
m_ph1 <- ms_model(prog = 0.08, death = 0.01, death_prog = 0.06,
                  switch_rate = 0.05, death_switch = 0.7 * 0.06)
d_af <- max(abs(ms_surv(m_af1, tt, "os")$surv - ms_surv(m_ph1, tt, "os")$surv))
d_af
#> [1] 5.551115e-17

The largest difference between the two OS curves over 48 months is 5.6e-17. When death_prog changes over time, the accelerated failure time effect also changes the time scale on which the hazard after the switch is read, and the two models differ:

m_af2 <- ms_model(prog = 0.08, death = 0.01, time_post = c(0, 6),
                  death_prog = c(0.08, 0.04), switch_rate = 0.05, switch_af = 0.7)
m_ph2 <- ms_model(prog = 0.08, death = 0.01, time_post = c(0, 6),
                  death_prog = c(0.08, 0.04), switch_rate = 0.05,
                  death_switch = 0.7 * c(0.08, 0.04))
os_af <- sapply(list(aft = m_af2, hazard_ratio = m_ph2),
                function(m) ms_surv(m, tc, "os")$surv)
rownames(os_af) <- paste("month", tc)
round(os_af, 3)
#>            aft hazard_ratio
#> month 12 0.716        0.718
#> month 24 0.479        0.483
#> month 36 0.325        0.328

Switching before progression

A patient who is progression-free may switch with the hazard switch_pre and enters state 5. There the hazards of progression and death are prog_switch and death_switch_pre; at progression the patient enters state 3 and dies with the hazard death_switch.

ctl_pre <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.10, 0.08), death = 0.01,
                    death_prog = 0.06, death_switch = 0.035, switch_pre = 0.02,
                    prog_switch = 0.06, death_switch_pre = 0.007, dropout = 0.003)
ms_prob(ctl_pre, time = c(6, 12, 24))
#>   time progression_free progression_free_switched progressed   switched
#> 1    6       0.47711392                0.06723685  0.3236912 0.01369166
#> 2   12       0.24659696                0.07873972  0.3638703 0.03572292
#> 3   24       0.06587475                0.05593000  0.2637657 0.06368279
#>        dead
#> 1 0.1182664
#> 2 0.2750701
#> 3 0.5507468

The column progression_free_switched is the probability of state 5. pfs_switch in ms_scenario() sets whether PFS is followed up to progression or death after such a switch ("event", the default) or censored at the switch ("censor", for example when the start of a new treatment censors PFS). The censoring appears among the PFS dropouts of ms_events():

acc <- ms_accrual(rate = 25)
scn_event <- ms_scenario(ctl_pre, trt_sw, accrual = acc)
scn_censor <- ms_scenario(ctl_pre, trt_sw, accrual = acc, pfs_switch = "censor")
ev <- rbind(event = ms_events(scn_event, n = 500, calendar_time = 24, endpoint = "pfs"),
            censor = ms_events(scn_censor, n = 500, calendar_time = 24, endpoint = "pfs"))
ev[, c("events_control", "dropouts_control", "events_treatment", "dropouts_treatment")]
#>        events_control dropouts_control events_treatment dropouts_treatment
#> event        169.6267         5.294087         134.7651           6.520328
#> censor       155.9178        35.881942         134.7651           6.520328
pfs_power <- sapply(list(event = scn_event, censor = scn_censor), function(s)
  ms_power(s, n = 500, looks = ms_looks("pfs"), test = ms_test(endpoints = "pfs"),
           events = 300)$power)
pfs_power
#>     event    censor 
#> 0.9582631 0.9776734

With 300 PFS events at a single analysis, the power of the PFS test is 0.958 when the switch does not change the definition of PFS and 0.978 when it censors PFS.

Censoring of PFS only

dropout censors both endpoints. dropout_pfs adds a censoring of PFS only, for example the end of tumour assessments:

ctl_dp <- ms_model(time = c(0, 4), prog = c(0.10, 0.08), death = 0.01,
                   death_prog = 0.06, dropout = 0.003, dropout_pfs = 0.02)
scn_dp <- ms_scenario(ctl_dp, trt_sw, accrual = acc)
rbind(pfs = ms_events(scn_dp, n = 500, calendar_time = 24, endpoint = "pfs"),
      os = ms_events(scn_dp, n = 500, calendar_time = 24, endpoint = "os"))[
  , c("events_control", "dropouts_control")]
#>     events_control dropouts_control
#> pfs      155.91779        35.881942
#> os        80.73701         8.383434

References

Robins JM, Tsiatis AA (1991). Correcting for non-compliance in randomized trials using rank preserving structural failure time models. Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods 20:2609-2631.
